catalog_quote: After analysing all available evidence, Maggi comes to the conclusion that Old Khotanese was a language with a 'quasi-fixed' stress. In general, he argues, the stress in polysyllables fell on the first heavy syllable from the end of the word (other than the final syllable, which was never stressed), while words containing only light syllables were stressed on the initial syllable. However, these rules are not absolute, hence the qualification 'quasi-'. In particular, Maggi states that words of four or more syllables with the abl. sg. m. ending -äna or the loc. pl. ending -uvŏ' are stressed on the antepenultimate syllable, even if this is light. ... [p. 21:] it is clear from Maggi 1992, §94, that metrical considerations provide the only evidence for his statement that the heavy final syllable of a polysyllabic word is never accented. ... new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Old Khotanese has an empty rule field, so this is the first placement statement held by the project: weight-sensitive right-edge stress (heavy penult; final light syllable never stressed) with morphologically conditioned initial stress in finite verbs and secondary stress in longer words. Nothing in the catalog to contradict.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is weight-sensitive and counted from the right edge: a word-final light syllable is never stressed, and words ending .HL or..LHL (the vast majority) carry the stress on the heavy penult (the Maggi 1992 / Emmerick 2024 rule: stress on the first heavy syllable from the end of the word, excluding the final). Sims-Williams reconstructs the system from metrical lightening: a heavy syllable that can be metrically lightened must be unstressed, so uysnōra HHL is HˈHL, handara HLL is HˈLL, aysmū HH is HˈH (he suggests all HH words may be stressed on the second syllable). Morphologically conditioned stem-initial stress overrides the weight rule in finite verb forms: ˈsarbīndä ˈHHL ‘they rise’, ˈsarbätĕ ˈHLL, ˈkṣamätä ˈLLL (the 3 sg. pres. of many type-A verbs), contrasted with häˈmätĕ ‘becomes’; he calls these ‘a more general set of rules regarding the stress of finite verbal forms’ (Sims-Williams 2022: 76-77). Unlike Emmerick he holds (per the compiler preface, held by the project) that final syllables with a long vowel or diphthong can be stressed (thaˈtau vs Emmerick’s ˈthato).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Stated explicitly: ‘many words of more than two syllables have both primary and secondary stress’ (p. 343) and ‘longer words have a secondary stress on which the an earlier reading may fall’ (p. 354); the metrical an earlier reading may coincide with either the primary or a secondary word-stress (n. 6, p. 333).
new_statements.exceptions: Finite verb forms with a heavy monosyllabic present/past stem plus HL ending (ˈsarbīndä) and 3 sg. pres. forms of type-A verbs (ˈkṣamätä ˈLLL, ˈsarbätĕ ˈHLL) are stressed on the first syllable, not the heavy penult; hīṣṭātĕ HHL ‘he sent’ lightens to hìṣṭātĕ LHL because the stress falls on the root *stā (two merged verbs), unlike pyūṣṭāndä; ˈuysanV̆ ‘breath’ has initial stress on the preverb (< *úz-anā-) contrasting with the cognate verb; English ˈadult ~ aˈdult cited as a parallel for doublets (n. 39, p. 352). The whole reconstruction is presented as a hypothesis inferred from metre, disputed by Fattori 2025 and Hitch 2014/2024, who deny that stress is a structural feature of the metre.
new_statements.identity_note: All statements concern Old Khotanese as attested in the Book of Zambasta (5th-6th c. CE, Khotan); Sims-Williams reconstructs ‘the system of word-stress in the language of the author’ of Z. Late Khotanese forms (LKhot. ˈhime, uysaṃdī) are cited only as comparative evidence. Emmerick’s Handbook rule is stated for Khotanese generally.

new_statements.quote: In contrast with the accent rules formulated by Maggi (1992), which implied a “quasi-fixed” stress in Khotanese, the author is of the opinion that “metrical and other evidence shows that Old Khotanese continues to be characterized by a free stress typologically comparable to the free accent of Vedic” (p. 23). However, it should be stressed that, as pointed out by the author himself (p. 73), these conclusions are limited to one text (the Book of Zambasta) and do not examine the problem from a diachronic perspective.

new_statements.relation_note: Type differs. The catalog codes Old Khotanese 'weight-hedged' on the strength of Maggi's quasi-fixed rule (stress on the first heavy syllable from the end excluding the final; all-light words initial) as summarized in Sims-Williams 2022 §2.3, and the verified statement held by the project (Sims-Williams 2025 IIJ) is read weight-sensitive. This review makes explicit that the very source the catalog cites rejects Maggi's quasi-fixed rules and argues for a free (lexically given, Vedic-like) stress whose position must be deduced word by word from the metre (book ch. 6 and Appendix 3 'Words whose stress can be deduced from the metre'). The reviewer himself does not settle and calls the hypothesi…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The review does not state a stress rule of its own. It reports two competing analyses of Old Khotanese word stress: Maggi (1992) formulated accent rules implying a 'quasi-fixed' stress (the weight-based rule the catalog quotes via Sims-Williams' summary), whereas Sims-Williams (2022, p. 23), deducing stress from the metrical an earlier reading of the Book of Zambasta (an earlier reading = primary or secondary word stress), concludes that Old Khotanese kept a FREE stress typologically comparable to the Vedic free accent; e.g. the 'handara-effect' leads him to read han'dara-, a'ysmū with second-syllable stress where Emmerick/Maggi expected initial stress. The reviewer adds that these conclusions rest on one text, lack a diachronic treatment, and that only future work on other Old Khotanese verse, Late Khotanese metre and the prehistory of Khotanese accentuation 'will allow one to prove or disprove the author's hypotheses'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Mentioned only in passing: the an earlier reading is taken to coincide with 'the word stress (primary or secondary)' (p. 56), and § 4.3.2 of the book treats the 'uysnorāṇu-effect' and 'primary and secondary stress' (p. 57); no placement rule for secondary stress is given in the review.
new_statements.exceptions: handara-effect (p. 56 fn. 6): hypermetrical 7-mora cadences lighten the third mora from the end (HLL or HH > LLL or LH), which Sims-Williams explains by an earlier reading/stress on the second syllable (han'dara-, a'ysmū) rather than the first; proclitic shortening of tcahora-/tcohora- 'four' (pp. 31-32); uysnora-effect HHL > LHL (Appendix 2). No systematic list of exceptions to a stress rule.
new_statements.identity_note: Old Khotanese as attested in the Book of Zambasta (anonymous Buddhist verse; Khotanese mss 5th-10th c. CE, Khotan oasis and Dunhuang); the reviewer stresses that the stress conclusions are limited to this one text and are synchronic (no Old > Late Khotanese diachrony).

tone_statements.quote: Место ударения восстанавливается с учетом исторических синкоп и апокоп. [...] Чрезвычайно вероятно наличие тонов, в позднехотаносакском многие слова (слогоморфемы) помечены особым знаком, передаваемым в транслитерации как [ʼ]; в этих слогах в дохотаносакском, а в некоторых случаях — в раннехотаносакском выпал шипящий или х, иногда рядом синкопирован другой слог. Предположительно для них можно реконструировать фарингализованный тон или своего рода просодическую «эризацию». Такая реконструкция ареально поддерживается соседством с китайским, тибетским и уйгурским языками и живыми засвидетельствованными контактами с ними.
tone_statements.translation: The place of the stress is reconstructed taking account of the historical syncopes and apocopes. [...] The presence of tones is extremely probable: in Late Khotanese many words (syllable-morphemes) are marked with a special sign, rendered in transliteration as [the subscript hook]; in these syllables a hushing sibilant or h dropped out in pre-Khotanese, in some cases in Early Khotanese, and sometimes a neighbouring syllable was syncopated as well. Presumably a pharyngealized tone, or a kind of prosodic 'erization', can be reconstructed for them. Such a reconstruction is areally supported by the neighbourhood of Chinese, Tibetan and Uyghur and by the attested living contacts with them.
tone_statements.locator: §5.1.0 'Фонологические сведения', p. 48 bottom - p. 49 top; stress examples on p. 49
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Hypothesis only: Late Khotanese syllables written with the subscript hook (from lost sibilant/h) carried a distinctive 'pharyngealized tone' or rhotacized prosody; no tone inventory; word stress reconstructed as variable (final/penult/antepenult by etymology and syncope).

readall_conflicts: Within the opened material there is one substantive disagreement about placement and one about the status of stress. (1) Placement at the right edge: Emmerick’s Handbook rule (2024: 9, §1.15-1.16, publisher sample held by the project) says stress falls on the first heavy syllable from the end of the word ‘but not on the final syllable itself’, and words with no non-final heavy syllable are stressed on the first syllable (ˈpharu, ˈthato, ˈhvatana); Sims-Williams (Reader preface, and the 2025 IIJ article) accepts the heavy-penult rule for..HL words and that a final light syllable is never stressed, but holds that all or most words ending in a syllable with a long vowel or diphthong are stressed on that final syllable (thaˈtau, aysˈmū HˈH), and that finite verb forms such as ˈsarbīndä, ˈkṣamätä, ˈsarbätĕ carry stem-initial stress regardless of weight. (2) Status: Fattori 2025 and Hitch 2014/2024, as reported by Sims-Williams, deny that word stress is a structural feature of Old Khotanese metre and hold the metre to be purely quantitative; Sims-Williams notes that Fattori nonetheless ‘seems inclined to accept that the difference between these two classes of HHL words was probably a matter of stress’ (n. 22, p. 343). All parties agree the language had a word stress; the dispute is over its exact position in certain word classes and whether the metre tracks it. The Dragoni review could not be opened, so its position is unknown. The one work opened (Dragoni 2024, OLZ 119/1: 55-57)…

sources.quote: §1.15 'Khotanese had a stress accent that lay on the first heavy syllable from the end of the word but not on the final syllable itself. A heavy syllable is defined as a syllable containing a long or nasalised vowel or a syllable ending in one or more consonants. Thus, yanīmä /jaˈniːmə/ ... is stressed on the penult ... because it contains the long vowel ī, while namaśtä /naˈmaštə/ ... is stressed on the penult because it ends in the consonant ś.' §1.16 'Words containing no heavy syllables or whose only heavy syllable is their final syllable are stressed on the first syllable e.g. pharu /ˈpʰar
sources.note: Current reference/teaching grammar edited by the two living stress specialists; sample already gives the rule (§1.15-16) with nasalised vowels counted heavy; full text would show any later-Khotanese or morphological qualifications and supersedes Emmerick 1989/2009 sketches on the Glottolog list.

Такая реконструкция ареально поддерживается соседством с китайским, тибетским и уйгурским языками и живыми засвидетельствованными контактами с ними.

tone.translation: The place of the stress is reconstructed taking account of the historical syncopes and apocopes. [...] The presence of tones is extremely probable: in Late Khotanese many words (syllable-morphemes) are marked with a special sign, rendered in transliteration as [the subscript hook]; in these syllables a hushing sibilant or h dropped out in pre-Khotanese, in some cases in Early Khotanese, and sometimes a neighbouring syllable was syncopated as well. Presumably a pharyngealized tone, or a kind of prosodic 'erization', can be reconstructed for them. Such a reconstruction is areally supported by the neighbourhood of Chinese, Tibetan and Uyghur and by the attested living contacts with them.

tone.summary: Hypothesis only: Late Khotanese syllables written with the subscript hook (from lost sibilant/h) carried a distinctive 'pharyngealized tone' or rhotacized prosody; no tone inventory; word stress reconstructed as variable (final/penult/antepenult by etymology and syncope).
tone.says: States (as a reconstruction) that Late Khotanese very probably HAD TONES: syllables written with the special sign transliterated as the subscript hook (where a sibilant or h was lost in pre-/Early Khotanese, sometimes with syncope of a neighbouring syllable) are reconstructed as carrying a 'pharyngealized tone' or a kind of prosodic 'erization' (rhotacization), with areal support from Chinese, Tibetan and Uyghur contact. tone.quote: It is only fair to note that these matters are highly controversial (cf. Hitch 2024; Sims-Williams 2025a; Fattori 2025a) and that my views on the position of the stress in Old Khotanese differ from those of Emmerick and others in important respects. For example, Emmerick took the view that no word bears a stress on its final syllable (Intro. §1.15), whereas in my view all or most words ending with a syllable containing a long vowel or diphthong are stressed on that syllable. Consequently, a word such as thatau ‘quickly’ is given in the metrical analysis here with a different stress (thaˈtau) from that suggested by Emmerick ([ˈtʰa’oː], Intro. §1.16).
